fields.description:
SERVER-50749 identifies some performance problems when loading data in py-tpcc.

In attempting to reproduce the problem, I saw some high latency  insert operations that seem to be caused by WT cache eviction pressure.

In particular, during a 25 minute test run, I saw 15 operations of 16+ seconds. All of these stalls correlated with aggressive eviction, high numbers of pages evicted by application threads, and evictions requiring restoration.

comments.body:
I was able to produce this issue using [~mark.callaghan]'s repro script from SERVER-50749.  I used the [WT py-tpcc how-to page|https://wiki.corp.mongodb.com/display/WT/Running+py-tpcc+locally] to get that tool installed and running on my virtual workstation. The one change I made was that I decreased the WT cache size from 40GB to 10GB, since my virtual workstation only has 16GB of RAM.  

Mark's script runs {{py-tpcc}} twice in succession, because he has been seeing a large (~25x) slow down between the 1st and 2nd run.  I didn't observe that behavior, but like Mark I saw a number of high latency insert requests [1].  In my case, I saw them during both runs of {{py-tpcc}}.  With 100 warehouses, I was seeing latencies over 10s, with one or two over 20s. With 250 warehouses, I saw latencies up to 40s. The behavior was similar with both MongoDB 4.4.0 and 4.4.1rc3.

I've attached the FTDC data from the first {{py-tpcc}} execution of a run with 250 warehouses.  In image below, I added pins at the time of all 15 operations that took > 16 seconds.  These correspond perfectly with spikes in various metrics:

!Screen Shot 2020-09-09 at 6.16.19 PM.png!

FWIW, the spike in the middle that doesn't have a pin corresponds to a 15.5 second latency. So it just barely missed my cutoff.

[1] Mark's mongoDB config file includes a command to log queries that take more than 5 seconds.  You can find those in the {{mongo.log}} by searching for "Slow query"

Based on a few more quick measurements, it appears this problem is exacerbated by large cache sizes.

I grabbed a ubuntu1804-large instance from Evergreen.  This platform has 60 GB RAM and 16 cores.  

I ran [~mark.callaghan]'s test from SERVER-50749, performing two runs of pytpcc doing load separated by a few minutes of sleep time.  I only used 100 warehouses.  I ran this test with a few different WT cache sizes ranging from 1 to 40 GB.

Results:
||Cache size (GB)||Load time 1
 (sec)||Load time 2
 (sec)||Load time
 Delta (sec)||num. inserts >
 5 sec latency||Max Insert
 Latency (sec) ||
|1|252|245|-7|0|2.5|
|10|221|247|26|12|16|
|25|210|333|123|21|68|
|40|244|466|222|17|164|

As in SERVER-50749, the slower second load is not consistent.  The table shows the second of two runs I did with 25GB cache. In the first, the difference between the load phases was only 26 seconds although the max latency was 31 sec.

They are intermittent and might be more likely on the second load but they can occur on either the first or second or both. There are a few results [here|https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-50749?focusedCommentId=3376240&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-3376240] where the stall happens on the first load for 4.4.0 when flow control is enabled

We addressed a similar issue running the same workload as part of WT-6444, the next step should be to revisit the changes made in WT-6444 and checking whether they are still working as expected in the latest version of WiredTiger and MongoDB
We discussed this one during planning today.  The plan is to look into this one once WT-6624 is merged.
[~brian.lane] do you remember the context here? I thought we'd fixed this previously independent of WT-6624, so I'm curious why it's waiting on WT-6624 now?

!compare-all.png|width=100%!

After several issues with multiple machines, I have data to compare between 4.4.1 and 4.2.10, both with 1gb cache and 40gb cache for two subsequent runs each separated by 600 seconds of inactivity.

!compare_different_versions.png|width=100%!

Here are a few more comparisons between various versions to help trace the timeline of this issue. It does appear that we have continued to make the issue worse.

It is noticeable that in 4.4 the throughput drops after an initial start and then stays very low, but very consistent. It appears like something is restricting it artificially. I compared the cache states and figured that flowcontrol is making this much worse:

!4-2-10-vs-master-flow.png|width=100%!

Here is a close up of what happens when the cache usage drops instead of being fully utilized:

!4-2-10-vs-master-closeup.png|width=100%!

Here is a run on a branch before WT-6490 was introduced (I am not sure if WT-6490 plays a role, but I am investigating):

!flow-on-vs-flow-off.png|width=100%!

[~sulabh.mahajan], it does look like flow control is playing a role, but a better metric to judge the impact is flow control timeAcquiringMicros. t2 displays the derivative of this divided by 1e6, which is the average number of threads waiting on flow control; compare this to other metrics like active threads, concurrent transactions, and various WT metrics reporting time spent waiting, in order to judge the impact of flow control relative to other bottlenecks.

Thanks [~bruce.lucas],

SERVER-50749 has already root caused that stalls in WiredTiger have been causing the flow control to be triggered in this workload. So I will continue to look at the workload with flow control disabled.

!flowcontrol-compare.png|width=100%!

*Note:*

*This ticket is not actively being worked on.*

*I am working on other tasks at the moment, and I put effort on this ticket as I find time between these tasks. The story points "1" per sprint reflect the amount of effort as well. The urgency for fixing this performance issue is deemed low at the moment, and we will switch to working on this ticket full time as and when the priority changes.*

To check if this is because of {{_dupKey}} performance dropping because of inefficient {{search_near}}, I decided to re-run the tests without having unique indexes. Following change to pytpcc:

{noformat}
diff --git a/pytpcc/drivers/mongodbdriver.py b/pytpcc/drivers/mongodbdriver.py
index 0482331..11911ba 100644
--- a/pytpcc/drivers/mongodbdriver.py
+++ b/pytpcc/drivers/mongodbdriver.py
@@ -327,7 +327,7 @@ class MongodbDriver(AbstractDriver):
                     continue
                 self.__dict__[name.lower()] = self.database[name]
                 if load_indexes and name in TABLE_INDEXES:
-                    uniq = True
+                    uniq = False
                     for index in TABLE_INDEXES[name]:
                         self.database[name].create_index(index, unique=uniq)
                         uniq = False
{noformat}

Here are the results - without using unique indexes:

||Version||FlowControl||Load 1||Load 2||
|4.2.17|ON|53m 15s|53m 28s|
|4.2.17|OFF|56m 37s|58m 20s|
|Latest Master (79370f1ea8)|ON|41m 2s|42m 30s|
|Latest Master (79370f1ea8)|OFF|34m 41s|39m 10s|

Here is the investigation so far:

The tests had hinted at performance being lost walking the history store. We know there are some standing issues with {{_keyExists}} check for unique indexes having to spend a lot of time scanning history store. So I ran pytpcc with and without a unique index and between versions 4.2.17 and the latest master. From the previous comment, it is clear that performance is actually significantly better with the latest version if unique indexes are not used.

Here is for instance FTDC comparing 4.2.17 and master, with and without a unique index:

 !compare-4.2and5.png|width=100%!

Summary:
* master performed much better than 4.2.17 without a unique index
* master with unique index had the worst first load phase, and the second phase never finished.

Let's have a look at some statistics comparing master with and without the unique index. The only difference in the runs is that one index that is unique in pytpcc has been switched to the regular index to isolate issues with unique indexes.

!Screen Shot 2021-11-12 at 4.29.02 pm.png|width=100%! 

A - 1st load phase finishes on no-unique index test run
B - 2nd load phase starts on no-unique index test run
C - suddenly performance restores for test with unique indexes
D - 2nd load phase ends on no-unique index test run
E - 1st load phase finishes on unique index test run
F - 2nd load phase starts on unique index test run

The statistics around history store reads are strikingly different. On average:
* When using unique indexes 893k times we walked history store and found nothing to return compared to 1.5 times with regular indexes
* The above statistic is close to next() calls and the calls that skipped less than 100 entries
* Over the duration of 1st run over 6 billion history store searches compared to 10k for both the runs with regular indexes.
* As far as I can tell cache contents don't seem to be a lot different, but eviction behaves very differently - more hazard pointers to go through, more forced evictions by application threads. Very likely because of consistent use of the history store table.

Unknown:
* I don't know what happens at C. Till C we have reduced performance - I think because application threads are just scanning history store and force evicting those pages all the time (50k/s). But suddenly at C the performance restores and there are no history store searches anymore.

Next steps:
* I think this is a problem we have seen elsewhere and have been trying to resolve - SERVER-56509. I can familiarise myself with the current state of where we are and this ticket and the linked ticket SERVER-50749 could likely be duped to an existing one.

I am closing this ticket as a duplicate of WT-7264. We have been working on a project that would help with search_near performance and fix this issue. In the meanwhile, there is a solution offered in WT-7264 - which MongoDB has not been able to utilize yet.
